messages.content:
Ah, sm_61 (Pascal/GTX 10-series) explains the pain. That architecture lacks hardware support for Bfloat16, which Unsloth uses by default. That's why it's fighting you.

The GGUF is definitely the path of least resistance for Pascal. It handles the lack of BF16/Tensor Cores automatically.

However, if you want to run the full LoRA adapter on sm_61, here is a "Legacy Compatibility" Dockerfile.
It forces the environment to use Float16 instead of Bfloat16 and disables the newer kernels that crash Pascal cards.

Dockerfile (Pascal/GTX 10xx Support):

 
FROM unslothai/unsloth:latest-cu121-torch240

WORKDIR /app

Install dependencies
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \
 transformers \
 accelerate \
 bitsandbytes \
 protobuf \
 sentencepiece \
 huggingface_hub

1. Force Bitsandbytes to use CUDA (Critical for Pascal)
ENV BNB_CUDA_VERSION=121
ENV LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$LD_LIBRARY_PATH:/usr/local/cuda/lib64

2. Force standard attention (Flash Attention 2 doesn't work on sm_61)
ENV UNSLOTH_USE_FLASH_ATTENTION=0

3. Force Float16 (Pascal crashes on Bfloat16)
ENV TORCH_DTYPE=float16

COPY Final-chat.py /app/Final-chat.py

Launch
CMD ["python", "Final-chat.py"]

 

One small tweak needed in the python script for Pascal:
In Final-chat.py, change dtype=None to dtype=torch.float16. Unsloth usually auto-detects, but on Pascal, hard-coding it prevents the BF16 crash.

If that's too much friction, stick to the GGUF q4_k_m. The quantization loss is minimal compared to the headache of running modern training stacks on 2016 architecture.
messages.why: Explains that Pascal/GTX 10‑series GPUs lack Bfloat16 support, affecting model execution.

messages.content:
Since I can't say it on reddit, I'll say it here: GLM 4.7 q8 is insanely good to me. Ive been running it on the Mac Studio; same speed as 4.6 and 4.5, but there is something so inherently different about the quality. I really want to see what context benchmarks look like, because more than anything else this model feels like it understands context better than any local model I've ever used.

In terms of inherent knowledge, it struggles with numbers still, , but that's about it so far. For example: I like to test these models by picking a handful of US and State statutes, and asking it about them. Like What can you tell me about 29 U.S. Code § 621? Just random ones. GLM 4.7 still gets those wrong almost every time, describing the wrong statute/law, but then if I ask for the statute by name instead (so What can you tell me about Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA)? ), it does a really good job.

In terms of conversation, it's the most human-like I've run into as well. It makes little choices in speech now that are just... I want to say harder to predict? But also more nuanced and human-like. Just exceptionally impressive.

Coding wise, it knocked out a search challenge that 4.5, 4.6, and every other local model I had used had failed; so I'm liking it there as well.

Maybe the honeymoon will end at some point, but so far I'm super happy with it
messages.why: Runs the model on a Mac Studio
